sentences.text: Net interest income plus noninterest income rose from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was a step change, not compounding: revenue was flat at $22.7 billion in FY2021 before jumping 15.8% in FY2023 to $28.0 billion [D117][D189][D169].
The FY2023 step came from higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition, which lifted net interest income 18.1% [D184][P33].
FY2025 net income rose 20.2% to $7.6 billion as noninterest expense fell 2.0% on prior-year merger and FDIC charges and lower compensation [D227][F30][D238][P10].
Payment Services was the steadiest engine, contributing +1.4pp of FY2025 revenue growth on 5.4% growth and a 25.8% revenue share [D261][D260][D259].
That segment's net revenue rose 5.4% on higher average loan balances, higher loan fees and lower funding costs, plus merchant and card volume [P4].
Consumer and Business Banking shrank 3.9% in FY2025 and subtracted 1.3pp, its revenue share falling to 31.0% [D252][D253][D251].
Its net revenue fell 3.9% on deposit mix changes and second-quarter 2025 loan sales [P6].
Operating costs fell 6.4pp more than revenue in FY2025, at -2.0% cost growth against 4.4% revenue growth [D238][D239].
The efficiency ratio improved to 59.0% in FY2025, below the 59.3% window median and far below the 67.4% FY2023 high [D220][D277][D276].
The FY2023 spike to 67.4% reflected merger and integration charges, MUB operating expenses and a $734 million FDIC special assessment [D170][P30].
The FY2025 recovery to 59.0% came from the absence of those prior-year charges and lower compensation from operational efficiencies [D220][P10].
Net margin of 26.5% sat 31.8pp below the 58.3% net interest income share, with the 7.7% credit provision and 59.0% efficiency ratio the gap [D223][D222][D221][D220].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; capital return is the better test [F60].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.7 billion in FY2025 equaled 48.3% of the $7.6 billion net income, down from $7.0 billion, or 100.8% of FY2019 net income [D218][F30][D65][F24].
Buybacks fell to $489 million in FY2025 from $4.5 billion in FY2019, while dividends rose to $3.2 billion from $2.4 billion [X85][X79][X95][X89].
The diluted share count fell 9.6% from 1,724 million in FY2016 to 1,558 million in FY2025, then rose 4.6% from the FY2021 low of 1,490 million [X66][X75][X71].
Return on average equity was 12.2% in FY2025, above the 11.8% banks peer median and in the 71st percentile of seven peers [D226][D283][D282].
The efficiency ratio sat in the 14th percentile against a 61.7% peer median, so the 59.0% level is a relative strength [D280][D281][D220].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits in FY2025, up from the 67.2% FY2021 low as deposit growth outran lending in the pandemic years [D224][D122].
The allowance was 2.0% of loans, above the 1.5% FY2019 level, and the credit provision was 7.7% of revenue against a 6.1% peer median [D225][D72][D221][D285].
Long-term debt is not reported after FY2022, a data break that blocks any leverage trend past that year [R2][X172].
The gap is a disclosure artifact rather than a balance-sheet event, but it leaves the debt path unverifiable from the pack.
Revenue fell 2.4% in FY2024 to $27.3 billion, the only decline in the window [R1][D194][D214].
The drop came from a 6.4% fall in net interest income as higher rates hit deposit mix and pricing [D209][P21].
One down year after a rate-driven step-up looks cyclical rather than structural, since FY2025 revenue recovered 4.4% [D239].
If the efficiency ratio in the FY2026 10-K moves back above the 59.3% window median, the FY2025 cost recovery would be reversing [D277].
If net interest income growth in the FY2026 10-K falls below the FY2025 2.2% rate, the loan-growth and funding-cost tailwind would be fading [D234].
If the credit provision as a share of revenue in the FY2026 10-K rises above the 7.7% FY2025 level, credit costs would be building [D221].
